1.pericope_label: And it came to pass, that, as the people pressed upon him to hear the word of God, he stood by the lake of Gennesaret, And saw two ships standing by the lake: but the fishermen were gone out of them, and were washing their nets.

schools.summary: Barnes deflates the boats into open fishing craft and cites Josephus for their number on the lake; Robertson holds that Luke has left Mark's order here and is telling in his own way the incident the others already gave; Lightfoot shows that teaching in the open was ordinary rabbinic practice and yet came to be forbidden by canon.
Gill assigns the two boats to Peter and Andrew and to Zebedee's family; Calvin traces the lake's Hebrew name to an adjoining city and notes the later corruption of the form.
Clarke objects to calling the vessels ships and describes the beach-net method they were built for.
Henry places the episode before the miracles that close the previous chapter and identifies it with the briefer accounts of the calling of Peter and Andrew.
Chrysostom explains the crowd's pressing as love rather than need, and adds that it was not the miracles only but the grace of his whole appearance that held them silent.

Ambrose has the crowd heeding neither time nor place and pressing on to the water's edge; Bede sorts out the lake's three names and then reads the two boats as the circumcision and the uncircumcision, with the fishermen as the Church's teachers.

debates.question: Where does this episode belong in the order of events?

positions.position: Before the two miracles closing the previous chapter; the other Gospels had the calling in view and omitted the draught
Luke has departed from his usual practice of following Mark; the renewed call came before the first tour of Galilee

debates.question: Where does the name Gennesaret come from?

positions.position: From the nature of the water, which raises a breeze on itself by its crossing waves
From an adjoining city named in the older history, the form altered as the language became corrupted

outliers.claim: Shows that teaching outside the synagogue was ordinary among the rabbis, one teaching a whole day in the street before the temple mount, and that a later authority nonetheless forbade it by canon and rebuked a colleague for it.

themes: And it came to pass, that, as the people pressed upon him to hear the word of God, he stood by the lake of Gennesaret,
And saw two ships standing by the lake: but the fishermen were gone out of them, and were washing their nets.

3.pericope_label: And he entered into one of the ships, which was Simon’s, and prayed him that he would thrust out a little from the land. And he sat down, and taught the people out of the ship. Now when he had left speaking, he said unto Simon, Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught. And Simon answering said unto him, Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net.

schools.summary: Barnes works out the acoustics of a cove and notes that sitting was the teacher's posture; Ellicott observes that this was a method used more than once; Robertson identifies the verb for putting out as a rare double compound; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic idiom for toiling all night.
Gill takes Peter's title to show he already knew Jesus for the Messiah and a teacher sent from God.
Clarke explains the move to the boat by the pressure of the crowd and thinks Peter meant both senses of the title at once, teacher and commander.
Chrysostom states the principle of the call: in his condescension he summoned the wise men by a star and the fishermen by their fishing.
Cyril reads the turn from teaching to miracle as deliberate, and notes the double kindness done to the owner of the borrowed boat.

Augustine uses the broken nets to distinguish this miracle from the one after the resurrection, where the nets held; Ambrose sets the two accounts of Peter's boat side by side as the Church first wavering and at last abounding.

debates.question: How much did Peter already know about the man giving the order?

positions.position: He knew him already for the Messiah, the king of Israel, a teacher sent from God
He knew little; Jesus came to these fishermen almost a stranger, which is what makes the obedience remarkable faith

debates.question: Is this the same miracle as the draught after the resurrection?

positions.position: No: different time, different side of the boat, and there the nets held despite the size of the fish, where here they break

outliers.claim: Calls the scene the most sublime imaginable, the Son of God preaching from the bosom of a placid lake that is itself an emblem of the peaceful influence of his doctrine.

themes: And he entered into one of the ships, which was Simon’s, and prayed him that he would thrust out a little from the land. And he sat down, and taught the people out of the ship.
Now when he had left speaking, he said unto Simon, Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught.
And Simon answering said unto him, Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net.

6.pericope_label: And when they had this done, they inclosed a great multitude of fishes: and their net brake. And they beckoned unto their partners, which were in the other ship, that they should come and help them. And they came, and filled both the ships, so that they began to sink. When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.

schools.summary: Barnes and Ellicott read the verb as inchoative or imperfect, the nets beginning to break, and Barnes notes that a real tear would have let the fish escape; Robertson dissents and holds the nets were actually tearing in two; Barnes also borrows a modern traveller's account of the kinds of net and of night fishing on that lake.

Gill identifies the partners and explains the beckoning by distance; Calvin states that the design of the miracle was to make Christ's divinity known and draws from it that labour undertaken on Christ's authority need not fear going unblessed.
Clarke supports the inchoative reading with a grammarians' rule that verbs of accomplishment often signify only its beginning, citing examples from Herodotus.
Cyril explains Peter's recoil by the crimes he recalled, and has him beckon because astonishment left him unable to speak.

Bede makes the fear proportionate to the gift, the more he feared the less he presumed; Augustine notes that Andrew is not named though thought to have been aboard; Ambrose turns Peter's words into an instruction to the reader, to confess and be answered with fear not.

positions.position: No: the tense is inchoative, they began to break, and a real tear would have lost the fish
Yes: they were tearing in two, which is why the second boat had to be called at once

debates.question: Why does Peter ask him to depart?

positions.position: Proportion: the more he feared the less he presumed
Law: recalling his crimes, he thought an unclean man could not receive one who is clean

outliers.claim: Draws a general rule from the miracle, that we need not fear our labour will go unblessed when it is undertaken by the authority and guidance of Christ.

themes: And when they had this done, they inclosed a great multitude of fishes: and their net brake.
And they beckoned unto their partners, which were in the other ship, that they should come and help them. And they came, and filled both the ships, so that they began to sink.
When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.

9.pericope_label: For he was astonished, and all that were with him, at the draught of the fishes which they had taken: And so was also James, and John, the sons of Zebedee, which were partners with Simon. And Jesus said unto Simon, Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men. And when they had brought their ships to land, they forsook all, and followed him.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the astonishment as seizing him, distinguishes the word for partners here from the one used earlier, and raises the harmonising difficulty that forsaking all creates; Robertson makes the Greek say a wonder held him round and notes the periphrastic future of the promise; Barnes weighs what the leaving cost as being everything they had; Clarke renders the promise as catching men alive and turns the call into a three-step method.
Gill fills out who was in the boats and who witnessed the catch.
Clarke contrasts fish taken to be killed with men taken to be preserved to eternal life.
Chrysostom measures the obedience by its timing, coming in the middle of the best fishing of their lives.

Bede takes the promise as especially Peter's own and reads the whole event as a picture of what goes on daily in the Church; Tertullian asks why the fishermen's trade was chosen and answers from a prophecy about sending fishers.

debates.question: Why were fishermen chosen for apostles?

positions.position: Because a prophecy had foretold that he would send many fishers who should fish men, and they understood he had begun to fulfil it
Because the promise was especially Peter's own, the taking of fish being explained as the taking of men by words

debates.question: Does forsaking all prove this is the same occasion as the call in the other Gospels?

positions.position: It is the strongest argument for it, but admits of a temporary return to the old trade, as happened after the resurrection
Little was left - two boats and nets - but it was all they had, which proves the love as fully as palaces would

outliers.claim: Renders the promise as catching men alive and presses the contrast: these fish are taken in order to be killed and eaten, while those converted under such a ministry are taken in order to be preserved to eternal life.

themes: For he was astonished, and all that were with him, at the draught of the fishes which they had taken:
And so was also James, and John, the sons of Zebedee, which were partners with Simon. And Jesus said unto Simon, Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men.
And when they had brought their ships to land, they forsook all, and followed him.

12.pericope_label: And it came to pass, when he was in a certain city, behold a man full of leprosy: who seeing Jesus fell on his face, and besought him, saying, Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean. And he put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will: be thou clean. And immediately the leprosy departed from him. And he charged him to tell no man: but go, and shew thyself to the priest, and offer for thy cleansing, according as Moses commanded, for a testimony unto them.

schools.summary: Robertson notes that Luke alone writes full of leprosy, evidently a far advanced case as a physician would see it, and observes the curious provision of the law treating the worst cases as less unclean; he also records the slip from indirect command into direct quotation.
Gill guesses the town and supplies the old physicians' description of the disease.
Clarke prefers a Galilean town and supplies a parallel from outside scripture, the gratitude-offering presented after recovery in another religion altogether.
Chrysostom explains the sending to the priest pastorally, since men remember God in sickness and grow dull on recovering.

Ambrose takes the unnamed city as the point, since not one people but all nations were healed, and holds that the priest was to learn the cure came by a grace above the law; Bede uses the healing and the withdrawal to distinguish the two natures and two operations in one person, against Nestorius; Augustine notes that the Lord appears to approve a sacrifice the Church does not require.

debates.question: Where did the healing take place?

positions.position: Probably Capernaum or near it
Some Galilean town, perhaps Chorazin or Bethsaida
No place is named, and that is the point: not one city's people but all nations were healed

debates.question: Why was the man sent to the priest with a sacrifice?

positions.position: So that he should keep God before his eyes and be certified clean by the priest's own inspection
So that the priest should learn the cure came not by the law's order but by a grace above it, the law being fulfilled and not abrogated
It approves a sacrifice the Church no longer requires, and must be understood of a time before the older order was superseded

outliers.claim: Uses the withdrawal to pray as a doctrinal instrument: it belongs to the nature that touched the leper, not to the nature that said I will, be thou clean - one person with two natures and therefore two operations.

themes: And it came to pass, when he was in a certain city, behold a man full of leprosy: who seeing Jesus fell on his face, and besought him, saying, Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean.
And he put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will: be thou clean. And immediately the leprosy departed from him.
And he charged him to tell no man: but go, and shew thyself to the priest, and offer for thy cleansing, according as Moses commanded, for a testimony unto them.

15.pericope_label: But so much the more went there a fame abroad of him: and great multitudes came together to hear, and to be healed by him of their infirmities. And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed. And it came to pass on a certain day, as he was teaching, that there were Pharisees and doctors of the law sitting by, which were come out of every town of Galilee, and Judea, and Jerusalem: and the power of the Lord was present to heal them.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that Luke agrees with Mark where the other account stops at the command, and that both verbs stand in the tense of continuous action; Robertson draws the consequence that the fame kept going and the crowds kept coming, and identifies the term for doctors of the law as one of the few apparent New Testament coinages; Barnes places the house at Capernaum.
Gill states the irony that the more the man was charged to keep silence the more he blazed it abroad, and reads the withdrawal as rest and private prayer.
Clarke argues from the Greek that the withdrawal was a settled custom rather than one occasion, and turns it into a charge to ministers who must receive before they can give.
Henry makes two points from the setting, that it was a weekday and not the sabbath, and a private house and not the synagogue.
Gregory Nazianzen presses that the works were done among the people while the praying was done in the wilderness, sanctioning rest from labour for converse with God.
Cyril rules out the reading that would make the healing power borrowed, and contrasts men who receive gifts and depart from the giver's rule with Christ, in whom the power went on abounding.

debates.question: Was the withdrawal into the wilderness a single act or a habit?

positions.position: A settled custom: the Greek is better given as he frequently withdrew
Rest from the fatigue of preaching and healing, and opportunity for private prayer
Not that he needed retirement, being God, but to show that there is a time for action and a time for every higher occupation

outliers.claim: Insists that the power present to heal was not borrowed from another but inherent, and contrasts men who become worthy of spiritual gifts and then depart from the giver's rule.

themes: But so much the more went there a fame abroad of him: and great multitudes came together to hear, and to be healed by him of their infirmities.
And he withdrew himself into the wilderness, and prayed.

And it came to pass on a certain day, as he was teaching, that there were Pharisees and doctors of the law sitting by, which were come out of every town of Galilee, and Judea, and Jerusalem: and the power of the Lord was present to heal them.

18.pericope_label: And, behold, men brought in a bed a man which was taken with a palsy: and they sought means to bring him in, and to lay him before him. And when they could not find by what way they might bring him in because of the multitude, they went upon the housetop, and let him down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus. And when he saw their faith, he said unto him, Man, thy sins are forgiven thee. And the scribes and the Pharisees began to reason, saying, Who is this which speaketh blasphemies? Who can forgive sins, but God alone? But when Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answering said unto them, What reason ye in your hearts? Whether is easier, to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Rise up and walk? But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power upon earth to forgive sins, (he said unto the sick of the palsy,) I say unto thee, Arise, and take up thy couch, and go into thine house. And immediately he rose up before them, and took up that whereon he lay, and departed to his own house, glorifying God. And they were all amazed, and they glorified God, and were filled with fear, saying, We have seen strange things to day.

schools.summary: Ellicott twice finds the physician's hand, in the technical word for the man's condition and in the diminutive used of the pallet that made the descent through the roof possible, and notes that only Luke has the healed man glorifying God himself; Robertson compares the three accounts on the faith, the form of address and the verb for forgiveness, and argues from a shared parenthesis that the three documents stand in some relation.
Gill takes the faith to cover both the sick man and his bearers, and limits those who glorified God to the common people rather than the Pharisees.

Clarke grants the objectors their premise and counts three miracles worked in their presence, each possible only to one omniscient and omnipotent; he also explains the crowd's word as meaning paradoxes.
Chrysostom argues the man's own faith from his consenting to be let down, states the argument in stages, and draws the moral that we neglect the soul's harm as we would never neglect the body's.
Cyril turns the objectors' premise against them: if none but God forgives sins, ask who but God searches the secrets of the heart.
Ambrose makes the knowledge of their secret thoughts the proof of divinity; Augustine holds that the word of forgiveness both grants what a man must need and shows who the speaker is.

debates.question: How is the charge of blasphemy answered?

positions.position: By three miracles in their presence, each possible only to an omniscient and omnipotent being
By turning their own premise: none but God forgives sins, and none but God searches hearts
In stages: disbelieve the forgiveness, then here is the reading of your thoughts, and then the healing of the body

outliers.claim: Takes the aside naming the man Jesus addresses, interrupting his words at the same point in all three Gospels, as conclusive proof that the three documents stand in some relation to one another.

themes: And, behold, men brought in a bed a man which was taken with a palsy: and they sought means to bring him in, and to lay him before him.
And when they could not find by what way they might bring him in because of the multitude, they went upon the housetop, and let him down through the tiling with his couch into the midst before Jesus.
And when he saw their faith, he said unto him, Man, thy sins are forgiven thee.
And the scribes and the Pharisees began to reason, saying, Who is this which speaketh blasphemies? Who can forgive sins, but God alone?
But when Jesus perceived their thoughts, he answering said unto them, What reason ye in your hearts?
Whether is easier, to say, Thy sins be forgiven thee; or to say, Rise up and walk?
But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power upon earth to forgive sins, (he said unto the sick of the palsy,) I say unto thee, Arise, and take up thy couch, and go into thine house.
And immediately he rose up before them, and took up that whereon he lay, and departed to his own house, glorifying God.
And they were all amazed, and they glorified God, and were filled with fear, saying, We have seen strange things to day.

27.pericope_label: And after these things he went forth, and saw a publican, named Levi, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he said unto him, Follow me. And he left all, rose up, and followed him. And Levi made him a great feast in his own house: and there was a great company of publicans and of others that sat down with them.

schools.summary: Robertson concludes from the different names in the three accounts that the man simply had both, and notes that the detail about forsaking all is Luke's alone; Ellicott catches an imperfect that extends the following beyond the moment; Barnes observes that the feast is missing from the account written by the man who gave it; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic name for the toll-booth and a parable turning on it.

Gill explains the walk out of the town as made in order to meet the man who was to be called, dates the feast later than the call on practical grounds, and reads Levi's motive as gratitude joined to a wish for his colleagues' good.
Clarke presses the completeness of the abandonment and turns it on the ministry, which must have no earthly entanglement.
Henry frames the section as a wonder of grace rather than of nature, and no less cogent a proof that Christ was sent of God.
Augustine identifies Levi with Matthew; Bede explains why the other evangelists spare the publican's name while Matthew accuses himself, so that no one should despair of salvation.

debates.question: Why do the Gospels name the same man differently?

positions.position: He had both names, and all three use the same phrase for the toll-place
The others spare a fellow evangelist the notorious name, while Matthew accuses himself so that no one should despair

debates.question: Why did Levi make the feast?

positions.position: Gratitude for the grace and honour done him, and a wish to bring his fellow publicans into the same company
Whatever the motive, he omits it from his own account

outliers.claim: Argues that the wonders of grace in this chapter are as cogent a proof of Christ's mission as the wonders in nature, to anyone who understands things rightly.

themes: And after these things he went forth, and saw a publican, named Levi, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he said unto him, Follow me.
And he left all, rose up, and followed him.
And Levi made him a great feast in his own house: and there was a great company of publicans and of others that sat down with them.

30.pericope_label: But their scribes and Pharisees murmured against his disciples, saying, Why do ye eat and drink with publicans and sinners? And Jesus answering said unto them, They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects the tense to were murmuring and notes that Luke keeps the objectors' own word sinners as they spoke it, and twice finds the physician's vocabulary in the proverb about those in health; Robertson reads the Greek as the Pharisees and the scribes belonging to them, and identifies the health word as the ordinary Greek term for soundness of body.

Gill takes the scribes to be those of the nation at large, observes that the reply answers a charge aimed at Christ though laid against the disciples, and presses that he did not merely call sinners to repentance but brought them to it.

Ambrose treats the question as the Serpent's own, the first word spoken to Eve being of the same kind; Augustine notes that Luke aims the objection at the Lord and the disciples together where the other accounts aim it at the disciples about him.

debates.question: To whom was the objection made?

positions.position: To the Lord and the disciples together, so the charge covers both
Nominally against the disciples, but Jesus knew it was aimed at him and took the cause up for both

outliers.claim: Identifies the murmurers' question with the Serpent's first word to Eve, and says that those who ask such things are diffusing their father's poison.

themes: But their scribes and Pharisees murmured against his disciples, saying, Why do ye eat and drink with publicans and sinners?
And Jesus answering said unto them, They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick.
I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.

33.pericope_label: And they said unto him, Why do the disciples of John fast often, and make prayers, and likewise the disciples of the Pharisees; but thine eat and drink? And he said unto them, Can ye make the children of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast in those days.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that Luke's form of the question is stronger than the plain form in the other reports; Robertson identifies the added verb of making, observes that the word for fasting often and the phrase about supplications are Luke's alone, and suggests the feast may have fallen on a fast day.
Gill records only that the days foretold came, and came very shortly.
Wesley draws out the force of the added verb, asking whether it is proper to make men fast and mourn during a festival solemnity.
Chrysostom states the reply in a sentence: the present is a time of joy, and sorrow is not to be mixed into it.

Cyril reads the second objection as a tactic and answers from the purpose of fasting, which is to quell the body's passions and was therefore not needed by Christ or by men made partakers of his grace.
Augustine reconciles the reporting of who asked, distinguishes a fast of tribulation from a fast of joy, and finds a darker point in the clause Luke alone records.

debates.question: Why did the disciples not fast?

positions.position: Because fasting exists to quell the passions, and neither Christ nor those made partakers of his grace needed it for that
Because the present was a time of joy and gladness, into which sorrow is not to be mixed
Because the question confuses two fasts, one of tribulation and one of joy, and the reply deals with each in turn

outliers.claim: Finds in the clause Luke alone records - that these children cannot be made to fast - a reference to the very men who would make them mourn soon enough, since they were about to kill the Bridegroom.

themes: And they said unto him, Why do the disciples of John fast often, and make prayers, and likewise the disciples of the Pharisees; but thine eat and drink?
And he said unto them, Can ye make the children of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them?
But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast in those days.

36.pericope_label: And he spake also a parable unto them; No man putteth a piece of a new garment upon an old; if otherwise, then both the new maketh a rent, and the piece that was taken out of the new agreeth not with the old. And no man putteth new wine into old bottles; else the new wine will burst the bottles, and be spilled, and the bottles shall perish. But new wine must be put into new bottles; and both are preserved. No man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better.

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that only Luke calls the illustration a parable and reports the sharper reading in which a piece is torn from a new garment to patch an old, and corrects two renderings in the wineskin verse; Robertson counts three parables in the answer, traces our word schism to the verb for tearing, and finds in the next verse a form appearing nowhere else in the New Testament; Barnes explains the last proverb from the taste of aged wine and applies it to the dispute; Lightfoot recovers what old wine meant in the schools.
Gill assigns the old bottles to the scribes and Pharisees and the new to the disciples and the sinners called to repentance.
Clarke explains the wineskins from the material, goat-skins whose old stitching would not stand fermentation.

Ambrose reads the old garment as fasting itself, on the strength of the apostolic phrase about putting off the old man; Augustine locates in the gift of the Spirit a fast of joy belonging to those already renewed.

debates.question: What does the saying about old wine mean here?

positions.position: That men who have tasted the gentler blessings of the gospel have no relish for the stern requirements being pressed on them, though the sterner duties will have their place in time
That old wine meant wine of three years, called wine of three leaves because the vine had leafed three times since
Fasting itself, which the apostolic phrase about putting off the old man tells against mixing with the new
The scribes and Pharisees, into whose hearts the new wine of gospel grace was never put

outliers.claim: Reports a better reading in which the patch is torn out of a new garment to mend an old one, and asks what folly could be greater than the act so described.

themes: And he spake also a parable unto them; No man putteth a piece of a new garment upon an old; if otherwise, then both the new maketh a rent, and the piece that was taken out of the new agreeth not with the old.
And no man putteth new wine into old bottles; else the new wine will burst the bottles, and be spilled, and the bottles shall perish.
But new wine must be put into new bottles; and both are preserved.
No man also having drunk old wine straightway desireth new: for he saith, The old is better.
